placeContext.headerLine: Jurisdiction not yet researched in this pilot

role.text: In view because this Story happens here.
The king in 1617 was Songtham, who reigned from 1610 or 1611 to 1628.
English company men were living here that year. One of them died here on 12 August.
The Dutch had kept a trading house here since 1608.
A Dutch merchant who lived here wrote in 1621 that the city surpassed any place in the Indies except China. He was arguing to keep his company's house open.
The marker shows the island city of Ayutthaya; it is not a surveyed position for any building of 1617.

entities.presentDayName: Ayutthaya, Thailand; the site of the village is not located

placeContext.headerLine: Jurisdiction not yet researched in this pilot

role.text: In view because the people who handled the hide trade lived here.
Historians place it south-east of the city. It may be as old as 1579 and was certainly here by 1617.
By December 1617 its people had a headman with a Siamese title.
Some of them had fled the wars in Japan, and some the persecution of Christians there.
No Source we have read marks the site.

placeContext.headerLine: Jurisdiction not yet researched in this pilot

role.text: In view because ships between Siam and Japan used this port.
A Siamese vessel arrived here in the summer of 1612, and the embassy of 1621 landed here.
No Source we have read names the port where the hides of 1617 were landed.
This port is also in the Story "The ship from Macao".
The marker shows present-day Nagasaki, an approximate location. It is drawn at the wider view only.

connection.directionFigureText: Japanese traders of Ayutthaya  →  enabled  →  the hide trade to Japan

spatial.targetText: Nagasaki · settlement precision · where a Siamese vessel arrived in 1612 and the embassy landed in 1621; no Source we have read names the port for 1617
spatial.routeStatement: Japanese ships came to Ayutthaya under the shogun's licence and went home with deer hides, rayskins and sappanwood. Japanese traders who lived in the city chose, cured and packed the hides. The ships brought copper and silver to Siam, by one clause in Baker and Pasuk; how much, no Source we have read says. The men who wrote about the trade in 1617 were Dutch and English merchants, and the Japanese traders themselves speak in nothing we have read.

connection.scholarlyStanding: Nagazumi (1999), Baker and Pasuk (2017), Reid and Clulow all describe a licensed Japanese trade to Siam between 1604 and 1635, and all take the count of 56 licences from the same Japanese study. Baker and Pasuk alone, among those we have read, say in so many words that copper and silver came back. None gives an amount for Ayutthaya.

mechanismText.text: The shogun wanted things Siam had: firearms, a scented wood, and saltpetre for gunpowder.
Japan was mining more silver than ever, and its ships could not trade in China.
A Japanese ship sailing abroad needed the shogun's licence. Fifty-six were issued for Siam between 1604 and 1635.
At Ayutthaya the ships loaded deer hides, rayskins and sappanwood.
Japanese traders who lived in a village south-east of the city chose, cured and packed the hides.
They had a headman with a Siamese title by December 1617.
The ships brought copper and silver to Siam, by one clause in Baker and Pasuk. No Source we have read gives an amount.
The Dutch came for the same trade, to earn Japanese silver, and were left with its poorer end.

This is how the Japanese traders of Ayutthaya made the hide trade to Japan work. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. Read together, the pages say this; no one Source lays out the whole of it.

participants.text: Japanese traders living at Ayutthaya, who chose, cured and packed the hides
Their headman, who held a Siamese title and is named by no Source we have read for 1617
Holders of the shogun's licences, and the shipowners who, Nagazumi reasons, sailed without one
Tokugawa Ieyasu, the retired shogun, who wrote first, in 1606
King Songtham, whose letter of 1621 says he had named an officer to look after the Japanese who stayed
The Dutch company's house, opened in 1608, and its head from 1617, Cornelis van Nijenrode
English East India Company men at Ayutthaya, who wrote about the price of hides
Hunters, woodcutters and carriers, of whom no Source we have read says anything

connection.evidenceIndependenceNote: The count of licences is one Japanese study, Iwao's, repeated by four of the historians here; it is one witness, not four. Baker and Pasuk's account of the Dutch at Ayutthaya rests on Bhawan and two others, and their 1621 quotation is taken from Bhawan. Clulow quotes the king's letter from Satow. Anderson and Satow both draw on the English Calendar of State Papers for 1617. The letters between the courts survive only as Chinese versions in a Japanese collection. No Siamese or Japanese merchant's own record is among the Sources.

reverseDisclosure.body: Copper and silver from Japan to Ayutthaya is the other half of this trade, and it is in this Connection's Claims, without an amount. What that silver did inside Siam, and what the hides did inside Japan, are different Connections with their own Sources. They are not researched here.

connection.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one.

jurisdictionLine.text: In 1617 Ayutthaya was the seat of King Songtham. The Japanese there had a headman with a Siamese title, and Dutch and English companies kept houses. How far the king's rule reached is not researched, so no boundary is drawn.

readingPaneEmpty.heading: One moment, and how we know it.
body: Select the Event on the map, or in the list beneath it, to open its Story.

This Moment is Ayutthaya in 1617: the hide trade with Japan, and the one Connection this pilot explains for it, the Japanese traders of Ayutthaya and the hide trade to Japan. Nagasaki is drawn at the wider view as the port where a Siamese vessel arrived in 1612 and the embassy landed in 1621. One part of the Story is about Japanese people who fled war and persecution, and about an attack on the royal palace in 1612.

segments.text: The amount of silver and copper. A ship's cargo list or a port's customs book would tell us. None is among the Sources we have read.
The hunters, woodcutters and carriers. The writers we have are merchants and courts; none of them wrote about the people who supplied the goods.
The headman of 1617. The one letter that mentions him gives his title and not his name.
The years between the attack of 1612 and the headman of 1617.
The king's letter of 1621 in the Siamese language. Only a Chinese version survives.

What a Siamese merchant, port officer or monk wrote in 1617. The one long history in Thai that survives from the Ayutthaya period stops at 1605, and the court chronicles of these years survive only as rewritten later.
